title: A roll of honor
hookLine: Var 11 lists the Sikhs of the Gurus by name and town, ordinary people remembered (Bhai Gurdas, Var 11)

lines: HARDLY ANYONE STOPS TO READ THEM.
A BOARD MADE OUT OF VERSE.
cards: On the wall of an old school hallway, or a fire station, or a village hall, there's often a board with names painted on it in gold. Hardly anyone stops to read it.
But somebody once decided those names should outlast the people. Bhai Gurdas made a board like that, out of verse.
One of his vars stops telling the stories of the Gurus and starts telling the names of the people who sat with them. Today: sangat.

teach.h: THE ELEVENTH VAR: A LIST OF NAMES.
teach.b: It's his eleventh var. Bhai Gurdas begins with the sangat, the gathering of the Guru's Sikhs, and what a Sikh of the Guru is like. Then he does something a reader might not expect.
He starts listing names. Sikh after Sikh, Guru by Guru, he names the people who came to Guru Nanak, then to the Gurus after him.

teach.h: A NAME, A TOWN, A TRADE.
teach.b: Often a name comes with something attached: the town they came from, their family, their trade, a nickname their neighbors would have known. Read it and you meet a crowd of ordinary people.
Not kings, not well-known holy men. People with work to do and towns to go home to. Why would a poet spend so many stanzas on a list?
Here's one way to hear it.

teach.h: THE SANGAT IS NOT A BLUR.
teach.b: A story about a great teacher can blur the followers into a background crowd that nods. Bhai Gurdas refuses the blur. For him, the sangat isn't scenery around the Guru.
It's made of particular people, each worth a line, each named the way their own town would have named them. And a list like this is a kind of witness. These people were there.
They heard the Guru's word, carried it home, and lived it in their own streets. One more thing.

teach.h: A ROLL THAT DOESN'T ASK RANK.
teach.b: In the Guru's house, a name on the roll doesn't depend on rank.
In Bhai Gurdas's list, being remembered comes from being a Sikh of the Guru. That's the whole qualification.

how: Sikhs read Bhai Gurdas's eleventh var as a record of the early sangat, and it's read and sung alongside the Gurus' bani in some gurdwaras.

games.why: in his eleventh var, Bhai Gurdas lists the Sikhs of the Gurus by name, often with their town, family or trade.

practice: Make your own roll: not well-known people, but the ones who carried you, a grandmother, a coach, the neighbor who fed you after school, a teacher whose name you nearly forgot.
Say each name slowly in your head and add what Bhai Gurdas would add: where they were from, and what they did with their hands. If you pray, you can hold each name for a breath.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: a Sikh, a learner of the Guru. Bhai Gurdas's roll names Sikh after Sikh.

carryVoice: Your line: ordinary names remembered. No rank needed to be on the roll. That's day seven hundred eight.
